items.title: Peel police union backs Alvin Tedjo in first ever endorsement of Mississauga mayoral candidate
items.summary: In their first endorsement of a mayoral candidate ever, the Peel Regional Police Association (PRPA) has endorsed Alvin Tedjo to become the next mayor of Mississauga. Tedjo has served as the Ward 2 councillor since 2022. He finished second in the 2024 mayoral race behind incumbent Carolyn Parrish, who is running again. PRPA represents over 3,800 uniform and civilian members of Peel police and said they are proud to stand beside Tedjo in a press conference Monday. “Public safety cannot be reactive. It requires leaders wiling to have difficult conversations before a crisis becomes tomorrow’s headlines,” said PRPA President Adrian Woolley. ” Before entering politics, Tedjo worked as a communications strategist for Toronto Metropolitan University and Sheridan College. The Mississauga mayoral race is expected to be a tight one with Tedjo facing off against Parrish, former mayor Bonnie Crombie, Tedjo and Dipika Damerla, who was the Ward 7 councillor. Parrish won the byelection after Crombie stepped down to become the Ontario Liberal leader. After failing to gain a seat in the 2025 provincial election, Crombie stepped down as leader in January. She announced back in June that she would be returning to Mississauga politics and running for mayor.

items.title: Police increase patrols in Mississauga, Brampton after shooting in Ontario city
items.summary: Police in Mississauga and Brampton say they’ve increased patrols around Jewish places of worship and cultural centres in Peel following a shooting in Belleville on Sunday night. m. after a Belleville Police officer came across an individual near Bleecker Avenue and Victoria Avenue, a mostly residential area of the city located about 180 kilometres east of Toronto. In a media release on Facebook, police in Belleville said both the police officer and the unidentified individual were injured and taken to hospital following an altercation. The incident appears to have unfolded near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue, during a gathering to mark Yom Kippur. The province’s Special Investigations Unit has been notified, and police in Belleville are providing no further comment at this time. The SIU is called in whenever serious injuries result from interactions between police and the public. ” Peel police added that during the High Holidays period, including Yom Kippur today, they have increased patrols around places of worship and cultural centres in Mississauga and Brampton.

items.title: Officer, 10 others hurt after fire breaks out in Mississauga apartment building
items.summary: A police officer and a firefighter were injured early Monday morning as they worked to help several people escape a burning apartment building in Mississauga, Peel Regional Police said. m. for reports of a fire near Inverhouse Drive and Lakeshore Road West. Police said the fire broke out in the hallway of a building. Firefighters, police and paramedics all rushed to the scene, where they found an apartment building on fire with several people inside. First responders went into the building and began rescuing people who were suffering from smoke inhalation. Acting Sgt. Amanda Steenson told reporters an officer and a firefighter were both injured during the rescue operation, which saw 10 people taken to hospital by ambulance. “One of our officers was reportedly injured as they were working to assist a firefighter with rescuing an individual from the residence,” she said. ” The cause of the fire is not known, and an investigation is underway. Police are yet to comment on the cause, but Steenson said suspect information could be made available later on in the investigation if it is deemed an arson.

items.title: Train tracks aren't shortcuts: cross safely
items.summary: Travelling on train tracks is illegal and dangerous. Always use designated railway crossings when crossing a railway track. Trains can move faster than they appear and may be much closer than you think. Following all railway signs and signals is one of the simplest ways to stay safe and avoid a potentially life-threatening collision. During Rail Safety Week, September 21 to 27, 2026, the City is reminding all road users to use Mississauga’s designated railway crossings safely and responsibly. With more trains and more people moving across Mississauga every day, staying alert at rail crossings is essential. Trains can travel at speeds of up to 140 km/h, and may require as much as two kilometres to come to a complete stop. Railway crossings have signs and signals to alert all road users of railway tracks and approaching trains. When approaching a railway crossing, always obey the lights, bells, gates and other warning signals. If a train is approaching or warning lights are flashing, stop behind the gate or marked stop line and wait until the train has fully passed. If the lights begin flashing after you have started crossing, continue across the tracks safely. Reminder, school buses are required to stop at least five metres from the nearest rail at all railway crossings, even if the signals are not flashing and the gates are open. While stopped, the driver must open the bus door and look and listen for any approaching trains. If you are driving behind a school bus, be prepared to slow down.

items.title: Suspicious fire at Mississauga apartment building sends 11 to hospital
items.summary: Eleven people have been taken to hospital following a suspicious fire at a Mississauga apartment building early Monday morning. m. Police said most of the victims suffered smoke inhalation and two people sustained serious, but non-life-threatening injuries. One of the people who was injured was an officer and paramedics say the injury is unrelated to the actual fire. The flames are now out and some residents have been permitted to return to their units. The cause of the fire has not yet been released but police say the incident is being treated as suspicious. “The scene remains secured pending the fire investigators determination,” police wrote in an email to CP24.

items.title: Renting in Mississauga? Here’s what to do when maintenance problems arise
items.summary: Know what steps to take when maintenance issues happen and where to get help. Heating problems, water leaks and pest infestations can become more difficult to manage as temperatures drop. This fall, renters may notice these and other maintenance issues in their homes. Knowing what to do and where to get help can make it easier to resolve problems before they affect health, safety and comfort. Whether you rent an apartment, basement unit, room or house, acting early can help prevent small issues from becoming bigger problems. Renters who know where to turn for help can often resolve concerns sooner. Rental homes should be safe and well-maintained. If they are not fixed, they can affect health and well-being. If you have a maintenance or property standards concern in your rental home: Many issues can be resolved when tenants and landlords communicate early and understand their responsibilities. items.title: Mississauga pauses new large-scale data centre development
items.summary: Mississauga city council has approved a temporary pause on new large-scale data centre development while the city reviews its planning policies and regulations for the sector. Council approved an interim control bylaw Sept. 16 prohibiting applications for new major digital infrastructure facilities with a total peak power demand of 10 megawatts or more for up to one year. The measure applies citywide and includes conversions and expansions of existing facilities. An interim control bylaw allows municipalities to temporarily prohibit a specific type of development while conducting a study to determine an appropriate long-term planning approach. During the pause, city staff will conduct a policy review of major digital infrastructure facilities, including data centres that house servers, data storage and networking equipment. The review will examine whether changes are needed to Mississauga’s Official Plan and Zoning By-law, as well as any new guidance or requirements contained in the Ontario government’s Data Centre Playbook. The city says there will be opportunities for public input during the review. An interim report outlining the scope and timeline of the study is expected to be presented to council later this year. Once the review is complete, staff will make recommendations to council on planning policies and regulations for data centres and other major digital infrastructure projects.

items.title: Woman wanted after 71 vehicles targeted in Mississauga break-in spree
items.summary: Police are searching for a woman wanted in connection with a series of vehicle break-ins across Mississauga. Police Regional Police say the incidents happened during the early morning hours of Sept. 3 and Sept. 6 in neighbourhoods throughout the city. Investigators allege vehicles were entered by smashing windows or through unlocked doors and valuables were stolen. Police say 71 vehicles were involved in the investigation. No vehicles were stolen and all were unoccupied at the time. Andrea Cederberg, 33, of no fixed address, is wanted on 23 counts of attempting to commit an indictable offence, nine counts each of mischief over $5,000 and theft under $5,000, and one count of theft over $5,000. Police say the investigation is connected to the recent arrest of Cory Lowden, 34, of no fixed address. Investigators have also identified possible connections to similar vehicle-related crimes under investigation in Halton Region, Toronto, York Region and Waterloo Region. Police say they are working with other police services across the Greater Toronto Area to determine the full scope of the alleged activity.

items.title: Nearly 9,000 students in Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon suspended over vaccine records
items.summary: Peel Public Health warned parents last year that students could be suspended from school over missing vaccination records. It wasn’t an empty threat. A total of 8,875 students were suspended in Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon during Peel’s 2025-26 immunization enforcement cycle, according to new figures provided by the region as thousands of students once again face scrutiny over their vaccination records. The number is significant because Peel Public Health is now warning that approximately 27,500 students will have their immunization records reviewed during the 2026-27 school year. The region says students with incomplete records could again face suspension if their information isn’t brought up to date or a valid exemption isn’t provided. The new figure comes months after Peel Public Health warned that 15,861 students were potentially facing suspension during the previous school year. At the time, the warning applied to students whose immunization records did not meet provincial requirements. Peel has now confirmed that 8,875 students were ultimately suspended during the full 2025-26 enforcement cycle. Peel says the 15,861 figure reported in March was a snapshot and changed from week to week as families submitted vaccination information. But the new number does establish something parents should take seriously: Peel does enforce the suspension provision.
